newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bankers say secrecy ease only for WW2 accts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bankers say secrecy ease only for WW2 accts.

text.p: Switzerland's decision to relax its vaunted banking secrecy to search for Holocaust victims' dormant wealth affects only a limited number of wartime bank accounts and is irrelevant for modern clients, bankers said on Friday.

They rejected as rumours in foreign exchange markets that banking secrecy itself on a broad scale was in danger and said weak fundamental economic factors, instead, were behind the Swiss franc's drop to 15-month lows against the mark.

The mark jumped from around 82.95 Swiss centimes to 83.70 late on Thursday as markets reacted to a media report repeating the Swiss government's request to parliament to suspend a three-month waiting period for voters to object to new laws. If parliament approves the request, Switzerland's strict laws on banking secrecy could ease as early was December or January 1 instead of April 1997.
At midday in Europe on Friday, the mark was up another notch to 83.80 against the Swiss franc.
"Banking secrecy, let's keep that very clear, will not be lifted for the vast majority of foreign and even local Swiss clients," said Swiss Bank Corp analyst Janwillem Acket.
"Banking secrecy is a fundamental fact which will remain as solid as our vaults," Acket said. "This is not going to be changed. This is a fundamental asset of Switzerland as a financial centre."
He dismissed "this very astonishing argument" on currency markets as "just plain gossip" spread by dealers to make money.

Union Bank of Switzerland chief economist Peter Buomberger was even more blunt, accusing Swiss banks' rivals of exploiting the current furore over the fate of Holocaust accounts to strike telling blows at the Swiss and try to woo away customers.
"Certainly, one dimension is that Swiss banks have many foreign competitors who are not unhappy to see this issue and would gladly see Swiss banking secrecy loosened," he said.

"I would not describe it as a conspiracy, this is going too far, but other banks in other countries see a chance for themselves in this matter," Buomberger said. "Competitors are trying to profit from this, so I can imagine there are lots of people abroad who want to play up the story out of concrete business interests."
Swiss banks deny allegations by Jewish groups and the head of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee that they are sitting on huge wealth left unclaimed by Jews murdered by the Nazis.

To help clear up the matter, parliament is set to give final approval in December to creating a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift banking secrecy in certain cases to help conduct a sweeping review of Switzerland's wartime role.
"The secrecy laws are going to be lifted only in cases where it is simply necesary to bring light into the dark of secrecy concerning the Holocaust victims' assets," Acket said.
"It is not going to touch any clients of the Swiss financial marketplace at all," he said. "This is only a small, minute detail which does not concern the normal Swiss bank client."

He and Buomberger said the franc was under pressure because the Swiss National Bank (SNB) had adopted an expansive monetary policy to try to weaken the Swiss franc and revive one of Europe's worst-performing economies.
SNB officials have made clear they consider the franc overvalued and will keep policy easy for the foreseeable future.

Acket said SBC saw the mark heading toward 85 centimes within a year. "We still see some room for a weakening of the franc against European currencies," he said. "Stay tuned for a further weakening of the franc."
CS Holding analyst Marion Swoboda said the franc was under pressure because investors were borrowing francs and selling them to invest in higher-yielding, longer-term assets abroad.
This was much more important than considerations about banking secrecy, she said.

"If things were laid completely open, if banking secrecy were abolished, then it is completely possible that people who have numbered acounts here would say they were pulling their money out and (the franc) would come under pressure. But I think there is no chance of it being totally relaxed," she said.
